title: Paul Whitehouse urges PM to act over ‘imminent extinction’ of Windermere’s ice-age fish
summary:
Experts say arctic char is threatened by pollution in England’s biggest lake as comedian unveils sculpture

  • UK politics live – latest updates

An ancient fish species that has survived in Windermere for more than 11,000 years is at risk of “imminent” extinction due to widespread pollution in England’s biggest lake, experts have warned.

New research reveals the arctic char (or charr) appears to have disappeared from large parts of the 11-mile long lake where its habitats have been eroded by sewage and other substances.

Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Endangered species Paul Whitehouse urges PM to act over ‘imminent extinction’ of Windermere’s ice-age fish Experts say arctic char is threatened by pollution in England’s biggest lake as comedian unveils sculpture UK politics live – latest updates Josh Halliday Thu 26 Nov 2026 05.25 EST Last modified on Thu 26 Nov 2026 14.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An ancient fish species that has survived in Windermere for more than 11,000 years is at risk of “imminent” extinction due to widespread pollution in England’s biggest lake, experts have warned. New research reveals the arctic char (or charr) appears to have disappeared from large parts of the 11-mile long lake where its habitats have been eroded by sewage and other substances. Andy Burnham was urged to act to prevent the loss of this “unique” species as conservationists erected an ice sculpture of the prime minister outside No 10 North in Manchester on Thursday. The 1.2-metre high structure, featuring a serious-looking Burnham between two blocks of sculpted arctic char, was unveiled by the comedian Paul Whitehouse , who co-stars with Bob Mortimer in the BBC’s Mortimer and Whitehouse: Gone Fishing. Whitehouse said the “imminent extinction” of arctic char in Windermere was “absolutely symbolic” of the pollution in England’s waterways. View image in fullscreen Researchers on Windermere in Cumbria. Experts say that while the arctic char is still present in the lake, it is in serious decline and faces extinction without urgent action. Photograph: Freshwater Biological Association/PA He said: “We need something to really highlight exactly what is happening, you know Windermere, the jewel in the crown of England’s freshwater resources – and it’s free, it’s available for everyone but it’s a basket case at the moment or it will be soon .” Whitehouse said Burnham had made “some positive noises about taking back control of our water companies” but that stopping sewage discharges could be his legacy: “This government and Andy Burnham could say, look, we cleaned up the water companies. What a legacy that would be .” Windermere, in the Lake District, has suffered from widespread raw sewage and bacterial pollution driven by discharges from United Utilities as well as 1,800 private septic tanks and private sewage treatment works. In March this year, the mother of a seven-year-old boy who kayaked on the lake described how he nearly died after contracting a dangerous strain of E coli from contaminated water. Experts say the arctic char in Windermere exists nowhere else on Earth because it has formed into four distinct populations since the last ice age more than 11,000 years ago. View image in fullscreen An arctic char. Some describe the orange-bellied species as like a ‘mythical creature’ or ‘ghost’. Photograph: Jack Perks/Alamy Its habit of lurking in the coldest depths of the 67-metre deep lake has led some to describe the orange-bellied species as like a “mythical creature” or a “ghost”. New research by the Freshwater Biological Association (FBA), published on Thursday, reveals that the arctic char appears to have disappeared from Windermere’s southern basin and was not detected in its historic spawning sites on the lake. The study, funded by Natural England, found that the char’s spawning habitats had degraded significantly since the last observations in 2017 because of an increase in sediment and algal accumulation linked to sewage. The first known written record of people on Windermere catching arctic char dates back to 1223, when Henry III was king of England. For thousands of years it was a prized delicacy and a key part of the Lake District’s economy, known to have been served to the royal courts of Tudor kings as well as local restaurants. A documentary about the demise of the char, called The Hunt for an Ice Age Survivor, was released by the campaign group Save Windermere on Wednesday. Matt Staniek, a zoologist who founded Save Windermere, described the char as the “canary in the coalmine” that warned of the rapidly deteriorating health of the historic lake. He urged Burnham to step in and halt all sewage discharges into Windermere, adding: “It is the epitome of the failure of government to protect our waterways from sewage pollution.
